question: What does the Bible say about faith and works?
intro: Christians read the New Testament as speaking of faith (trust in God and in Christ) and of works (what people do), and they join the two in different ways when they ask how a person comes to be right with God and how that person is finally saved. This page sets the main readings side by side, each in the words its holders use, and chooses none of them.

agreed.summary: Every reading below takes the text to say that salvation is God's gift by grace, that it is received through faith, and that the people God saves are made for good works and are expected to do them. The readings differ in how they relate faith and works when the text speaks of being declared righteous and of final salvation.

passages.quote: For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God,
For we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.
to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.

readings.label: Faith working through love: salvation is God's gift, and works done in God's grace belong to the life of the one he saves
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak of a faith that is alive in love, and of works that God himself enables, as together belonging to being made righteous and to final salvation. Catholic teaching understands justification as God making a person righteous as well as declaring them so, and speaks of works done in grace as bearing fruit and earning reward by that same grace. Catholic teaching holds that the first grace of justification cannot be merited by anyone (Catechism 2010). Eastern Orthodox readers speak of a lifelong cooperation with God's grace (what is called synergy), set in terms of healing and union with God. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) states justification as by faith working through love and does not accept faith alone as the whole account. Members of other traditions, Anglican members among them, hold parts of this reading.

passages.quote: What matters is faith expressing itself through love.
passages.note: Read as naming the faith that counts: faith made active in love.

passages.quote: As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.
passages.note: Read as naming deeds as part of what justifies.

passages.quote: You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did.
passages.note: Faith and action working together, and faith brought to completion.

passages.quote: Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food.
passages.note: Faith tested in practice: James 2:14-17 asks what good faith is when a brother or sister is in need.

passages.quote: it is the doers of the law who will be declared righteous.
passages.note: Read as saying that doing, as well as hearing, belongs to being declared righteous.

passages.quote: continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling.
passages.note: Salvation as something believers are told to work out.

passages.quote: For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose.
passages.note: The working is also God's: grace and the believer's acting together.

passages.quote: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.
passages.note: Quotes Genesis 15:6 and names Abraham’s works with it (James 2:21-22): read as faith and deeds belonging together.

passages.quote: will repay each one according to his deeds
passages.note: Paul says God will repay each person according to what he has done.

passages.quote: but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven
passages.note: Jesus says not everyone who calls him Lord enters the kingdom, but the one who does his Father's will.

passages.quote: faith without deeds is dead
passages.note: James compares faith without deeds to a body without a spirit.

passages.quote: each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad
passages.note: Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat and receive what is due for what was done in the body.

passages.quote: I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat
passages.note: In Jesus' account of the judgment, the king recalls being hungry and fed, thirsty and given drink, a stranger and taken in.

passages.quote: if I have absolute faith so as to move mountains, but have not love, I am nothing
passages.note: Paul says faith that moves mountains is nothing without love.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take the verses that exclude works (Romans 3:28, Ephesians 2:9, Titus 3:5) to exclude works done before grace or apart from it, or the observances of the Mosaic law, and not the works that grace produces in the believer. They take Romans 4:4-5 to speak of wages earned as a debt, which no one can claim before God. Holders of this reading also point to Genesis 22:18, where the blessing of the nations comes “because you have obeyed My voice”, and read the offering of Isaac in that light.

readings.label: By faith alone (what is called sola fide): God declares the believer righteous through faith in Christ, and good works follow as faith's fruit
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to teach that a person stands righteous before God through faith in Christ and that works contribute nothing to that standing. Righteousness is credited to the believer from Christ (what is called imputation), and good works follow as the fruit and evidence of a faith that is alive. Lutheran and Reformed readers state this as the center of the gospel, each with their own account of the law and of perseverance. Southern Baptists (the Baptist Faith and Message 2000) and Baptists of the 1689 London Confession state justification by faith in their own confessions, and other Baptist and free-church readers hold it. The Church of England's Article XI states it, as do many Anglican members, who differ in how they put it, and some set baptism and the sacraments close beside faith. The Articles of Religion of the United Methodist Church state it in these words (Article IX: justified by faith only; Article X: good works are its fruit), and the Global Methodist Church names the Articles of Religion among its doctrinal standards; both add the account of holiness set out in the next reading. The Assemblies of God and the Foursquare Church state justification by faith with Christ's righteousness credited to the believer, and teach sanctification as a continuing work.

passages.quote: For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
passages.note: Justification by faith, with works of the law set aside.

passages.quote: Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.
passages.note: Quotes Genesis 15:6 (“Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”). Holders of this reading take Paul to show there that righteousness was credited to Abraham for believing, before any work.

passages.quote: However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.
passages.note: The one who does not work, and believes, has righteousness credited.

passages.quote: a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ.
passages.note: Justification set on faith in Christ and not on works of the law.

passages.quote: Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.”
passages.note: The righteous live by faith.

passages.quote: not by works, so that no one can boast.
passages.note: Works excluded, so that boasting is excluded.

passages.quote: He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
passages.note: Salvation by mercy and not by righteous deeds.

passages.quote: And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.
passages.note: Read as setting grace and works as different grounds that do not mix.

passages.quote: Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness
passages.note: The Old Testament verse Paul quotes in Romans 4: Abram believed and it was credited to him as righteousness.

passages.quote: faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead
passages.note: James says faith that results in no action is dead.

passages.quote: since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God
passages.note: Paul says those justified through faith have peace with God through Jesus Christ.

passages.quote: justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus
passages.note: Paul says people are justified freely, by God's grace, through the redemption in Christ.

passages.quote: not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ
passages.note: Paul wants to be found in Christ with the righteousness from God that rests on faith, not his own from the law.

passages.quote: no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law
passages.note: Paul says no one is justified in God's sight by works of the law, which only bring awareness of sin.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take James 2:24 to use “justified” for being shown righteous: Abraham's offering of Isaac displayed the faith that Genesis 15:6 had already credited (James 2:21-23), and James is describing what real faith looks like in life. They take Romans 2:6, Romans 2:13 and 2 Corinthians 5:10 to describe the judgment that reveals the faith by which a person was already justified, and Philippians 2:12-13 to describe sanctification, in which God is the one working. They take John 3:36 to set belief against refusal to believe, and to promise life to the one who believes. They take James 2:17 and 2:26 to describe the faith that is alive, which does not remain without deeds, and Matthew 7:21 and 25:35-36 to describe what the judgment shows of those who belong to Christ.

readings.label: Faith as obedient trust: believing and obeying are one response to God, and holiness of life belongs to the way of salvation
readings.summary: Readers who hold this take the New Testament to speak of faith as trust that includes obedience, as in “the obedience that comes from faith” of Romans 1:5, so that following Christ is the shape faith takes in life and not an addition to it. Wesleyan and Methodist readers affirm that a person is justified by faith, faith being the only condition of justification (Wesley), with repentance and works necessary in another sense, for growth and for continuing in salvation; they hold that holiness of heart and life belongs to the continuing way of salvation, which a believer is called to keep, and from which, Wesleyan writers hold, a believer can fall away. Anabaptist readers speak of faith as discipleship, the daily following of Christ, with weight on the commands of Jesus. The 1995 Mennonite confession uses justification by faith as one name for salvation, says salvation is by grace and not by merit, and holds faith and faithful obedience to the covenant to be inseparable; Anabaptist members differ on how they relate discipleship to the word justification. Pentecostal and Charismatic readers, many of whose movements grew out of the holiness revivals, including the Azusa Street revival led by an African American preacher, share much of this. The Church of God (Cleveland) declaration speaks of sanctification as a work after the new birth, with holiness as the standard of life, while the Assemblies of God and the Foursquare Church state the second reading, with a call to lifelong obedience.

passages.quote: to call all those among the Gentiles to the obedience that comes from faith.
passages.note: Faith and obedience named together as the aim of Paul's apostleship.

passages.quote: And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him
passages.note: Eternal salvation for those who obey.

passages.quote: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life.
passages.note: The Greek word the Berean renders “rejects” (apeithōn) can mean refusing to believe or refusing to obey, and the site’s word-by-word gloss is “not obeying”. Holders of this reading take it as setting believing and obeying side by side; others take it as the opposite of believing, and cite the verse’s first sentence for life given to the one who believes.

passages.quote: will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of My Father in heaven.
passages.note: Entering the kingdom tied to doing the Father's will.

passages.quote: Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord.
passages.note: Holiness named as something to pursue, with the Lord's sight as its end.

passages.quote: you are slaves to the one you obey, whether you are slaves to sin leading to death, or to obedience leading to righteousness?
passages.note: Obedience leading to righteousness.

passages.quote: For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.
passages.note: Life tied to putting the deeds of the body to death by the Spirit.

passages.quote: So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.
passages.note: Faith by itself, without action, is dead.

passages.quote: offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God
passages.note: On account of God's mercy, Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices.

passages.quote: present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life
passages.note: Paul tells believers to present themselves, and the parts of their bodies, to God as instruments of righteousness.

passages.quote: continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling
passages.note: Paul urges believers who have always obeyed to keep working out their salvation with fear and trembling.

passages.quote: If you love Me, you will keep My commandments
passages.note: Jesus ties love for him to keeping his commandments.

passages.quote: everyone who hears these words of Mine and acts on them is like a wise man
passages.note: Jesus says the one who hears his words and acts on them is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.

readings.answers: Holders of this reading take Paul's “not by works” passages (Romans 3:28, Galatians 2:16, Ephesians 2:9) to exclude earning and the works of the law as a way to earn or as marks of belonging, and to leave open the obedience of trust that Romans 1:5 names. They take Romans 4:4-5 to place the ground of salvation in God's grace, with faith that obeys as the way it is received.

terms.note: The Lutheran and Reformed phrase for the teaching that a person is justified through faith with no contribution from works. Reformed teaching adds that this faith is never alone: the Westminster Confession (11.2), the standard of the Presbyterian Church in America and the Orthodox Presbyterian Church, says it is always accompanied by the other saving graces and works by love, and the Heidelberg Catechism (Question 64), held by the Christian Reformed Church, says it is impossible for those grafted into Christ by true faith not to bear fruits of gratitude.
The Lutheran and Reformed term for the righteousness of Christ credited to the believer.

terms.term: faith formed by love (fides caritate formata)
terms.note: The Catholic phrase for faith made complete in love, drawing on Galatians 5:6.

The Catholic term for the reward that God's grace makes due to works done in grace. Lutheran writers reject the term for forgiveness, grace and justification, though the Lutheran Apology uses it of the rewards God promises to believers' works; Reformed writers reject the term, holding that no work of the believer makes a person's standing before God due.
The Eastern Orthodox term for the human will cooperating with God's grace.
Growth in holiness after justification; Lutheran, Reformed and Wesleyan readers each use the word with their own account of what it involves.
The Anabaptist word for faith lived as following Christ.

Paul’s phrase in Romans 3:28 and Galatians 2:16. Traditions and scholars differ over whether it means good works in general, the Mosaic law as a whole, or the practices that marked Jewish identity (the last often called the New Perspective on Paul); each sense is held by some Christian readers and some scholars.

Paul (Romans 4:3) and James (James 2:23) both quote Genesis 15:6, “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness.” The readings differ over what it shows: righteousness credited for believing before any work, or a faith that Abraham's later obedience brought to completion (James 2:22). In the Hebrew Scriptures' own words, Genesis 22:12 (“now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me”, said by the angel of the LORD, 22:11-12) and Genesis 26:5 (“because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws”, the LORD to Isaac, 26:2-5) speak of Abraham's fear of God and obedience. The Hebrew of 15:6 has an active verb, “he reckoned it to him”, and the verse does not name who reckoned.

further_reading.title: Council of Trent, Session 6, Decree on Justification, chapters 7, 8 and 16 and canon 9
further_reading.says: It teaches that justification renews a person as well as forgiving sins, that faith begins it freely, that good works done in grace are meritorious as God's gift, and it condemns the view that faith alone justifies with no cooperation of the will.

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1987-1995 (Grace and Justification: Justification)
further_reading.says: It teaches that justification is not only the remission of sins but also the sanctification and renewal of the interior man (1989), that it is conferred in Baptism (1992), and that it establishes cooperation between God's grace and man's freedom (1993).

further_reading.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 2006-2011 (Grace and Justification: Merit)
further_reading.says: It teaches that merit before God comes from God's own invitation to share his grace, and that the first grace of justification cannot be earned (2010).

further_reading.title: Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), Decree 13
further_reading.says: It states that a person is justified by faith that works through love and not by faith alone, with works as the fruits through which faith becomes effective.

further_reading.title: The Longer Catechism of Philaret of Moscow, questions 481-484
further_reading.says: It teaches that true faith produces love and good works, that faith without them is lifeless, and that the strength to do good comes through faith-given grace.

further_reading.title: Augsburg Confession, Article IV (Of Justification)
further_reading.says: It teaches that people are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, and not by their own strength, merits or works.

further_reading.title: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Article IV (II) (Of Justification), especially paragraphs 19-26
further_reading.says: It denies that anyone merits the forgiveness of sins by works, and sets aside the scholastic division of merit into two kinds.

further_reading.title: Apology of the Augsburg Confession, Article IV-b (Of Love and the Fulfilling of the Law), paragraphs 73-75
further_reading.says: It teaches that good works are meritorious, not for the remission of sins, grace or justification, which are obtained only by faith, but for other rewards, bodily and spiritual, in this life and after it (paragraph 73).

further_reading.title: Luther's Large Catechism, Part Second (the Creed), Third Article
further_reading.says: It teaches that the Holy Spirit makes people holy through the Gospel and the Church, that holiness is not earned by works, and that faith given by grace moves believers to keep God's commandments.

further_reading.title: Martin Luther, Concerning Christian Liberty (The Freedom of a Christian), 1520, part 3
further_reading.says: Luther argues that faith alone makes a person righteous, that good works come from the justified person and never earn justification, and that a Christian still does them in service to the neighbor.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Confession of Faith, chapter 11 (Of Justification) and chapter 16 (Of Good Works)
further_reading.says: Chapter 11.2 calls faith the alone instrument of justification that is never alone in the person justified, since it is always accompanied by the other saving graces and works by love.

further_reading.body: Presbyterian Church in America and Orthodox Presbyterian Church
further_reading.title: Westminster Shorter Catechism, questions 33 and 35
further_reading.says: Question 33 teaches that God counts sinners righteous only for Christ's righteousness credited to them and received by faith alone, and question 35 teaches that sanctification renews the whole person to live righteously.

further_reading.title: Heidelberg Catechism, questions 60-64
further_reading.says: It teaches that faith alone receives Christ's righteousness, that even our best works are imperfect and cannot make us righteous, and that those grafted into Christ by true faith cannot fail to bear fruits of gratitude.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, chapter 11 (Of Justification by Faith)
further_reading.says: Calvin defines justification as acceptance for the righteousness of Christ received by faith, and holds that works cannot be joined to faith as a ground of justification.

further_reading.title: John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, chapter 16 (Refutation of the Calumnies Against This Doctrine)
further_reading.says: Calvin answers the charge that justification by faith destroys good works by holding that Christ justifies no one without also sanctifying them.

further_reading.title: Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion, Articles XI to XIV
further_reading.says: Article XI counts a person righteous before God for Christ's merit received through faith and not for their own deeds, and Article XII calls good works the fruit of a living faith that follows justification.

further_reading.title: To Be a Christian: An Anglican Catechism (2019), question 360
further_reading.says: The catechism speaks of a person as justified, declared righteous by God, and joins faith, repentance and baptism.

further_reading.title: Articles of Religion of the Methodist Church, Articles IX to XII
further_reading.says: Article IX counts people righteous for Christ's merit received by faith and not for their own works, Article X calls good works the fruit that shows a true faith, and Article XII allows those who fall after justification to repent and be restored.

further_reading.title: Global Methodist Church, Doctrinal Standards: the Articles of Religion and the Confession of Faith
further_reading.says: The Global Methodist Church names the Articles of Religion and the Confession of Faith as its doctrinal standards.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 5 (Justification by Faith)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that justification is God's pardon of the ungodly, that faith is its only necessary condition, and that good works follow as its fruit.

further_reading.title: John Wesley, Standard Sermons, Sermon 43 (The Scripture Way of Salvation)
further_reading.says: Wesley teaches that faith is the only condition of both justification and sanctification, and that repentance and good works are necessary as fruits that help a believer grow and continue.

further_reading.title: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article IV (Salvation), section B (Justification)
further_reading.says: It describes justification as God's gracious acquittal of sinners who repent and believe in Christ, bringing them into a favorable relationship with God.

further_reading.title: Second London (Baptist) Confession of 1689, chapter 11 (Of Justification)
further_reading.says: Paragraph 2 calls faith the alone instrument of justification, adding that it is never alone in the justified person but is a living faith that works by love.

further_reading.title: Assemblies of God position paper, The Assurance of Salvation (2017), sections II and IV
further_reading.says: The paper teaches salvation by grace through faith with Christ's righteousness credited to the believer (section II), and it holds that salvation can be forfeited by willfully turning from Christ (section IV).

further_reading.title: Foursquare Declaration of Faith, articles VII and VIII
further_reading.says: The Declaration says the believer has the righteousness of the Redeemer imputed to him (article VII) and that it is the will of God that we be sanctified daily (article VIII).

further_reading.title: Church of God Declaration of Faith
further_reading.says: It teaches that justification, regeneration and the new birth come by faith in the blood of Christ, that sanctification is a work after the new birth, and that holiness is the standard of life for God's people.

further_reading.title: Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective (1995), Article 8 (Salvation), commentary
further_reading.says: It teaches that salvation is a gift of grace and not a reward for goodness, and that justification by faith and faithful obedience to the covenant are inseparable.

_why: QUOTES: every quote was read against http://localhost:8012/api/verse and ticked: Eph 2:8, 2:9, 2:10; Titus 2:14, 3:5; Gal 2:16 (server text begins 'know that a man...', I quote the clause from 'a man is not justified'), 3:11, 5:6; Rom 1:5, 2:6, 2:13 (clause), 3:28, 4:3 (without the closing curly quote), 4:5, 6:16 (clause), 8:13, 11:6; Jas 2:17, 2:22, 2:24; Phil 2:12 (clause), 2:13; 1 Cor 15:10 (clause; the server's hyphen kept as is); Heb 5:9, 12:14; John 3:36 (first two sentences); Matt 7:21 (clause from 'will enter'). All ticked. I did not quote Rom 16:26 (it carries a manuscript note). ORDER: by when each reading was held and articulated, as I read the history. First: the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox reading, which runs from the early centuries (Catholic formal statement came at Trent, 1547, after the Reformation, but the reading it states is the older one in the church's life). Second: the Reformation reading (from 1517). Third: the Anabaptist (from the 1520s) and Wesleyan (1700s) reading. The ordering is by history and does not rank. THREE READINGS, NOT TWO: faith-alone and faith-plus-works is the familiar split, yet it leaves out the Wesleyan and Anabaptist positions, which affirm justification by faith and press obedience. I put those in the third reading so that no reader finds their view folded into an opponent's. PASSAGES: 14, 14 and 13 after the 2026-10-26 verse audit (eight each before it). HELD_BY: assignments are approximate and the summaries say where a tradition holds a reading only in part or its members differ (Anglican in 1 and 2; Pentecostal in 3; Wesleyans appear in 2's summary). Nothing names a person, scholar or leader. WORDS: I checked the summaries, answers and notes for 'but', 'however', 'actually', 'clearly', 'only', 'merely'. 'And not' appears a few times in descriptions of what a tradition teaches; it states that tradition's own contrast and is not a verdict. I removed the one 'only' from the summaries. Reviewers who object can reword. 'Only' also appears inside a quote (Matt 7:21), which is the verse's own word. 'Works of the law' is left as a term with three scholarly senses and no pick. LEFT OUT: (a) Jas 2:14, Rom 4:2 and Rom 4:4 are not passages; the verse audit of 2026-10-26 added 2 Cor 5:10, Jas 2:15, 2:22, 2:23 and 2:26, Matt 25:35, Phil 3:9 and Rom 3:20, among others. (b) The rest of the judgment of the nations (Matt 25:36 onward) is cited in reading 2's answers, not shown as a passage. (c) Gen 15:6 is now a passage of reading 2 (and Rom 4:3 quotes it); Gen 22 and the Jewish reading of Abraham's faithfulness there are not given a place of their own; a rabbi reviewing should say whether it needs one. (d) The question of whether eternal security holds or is lost: only touched in reading 3's summary as an attributed Wesleyan teaching; it deserves a card of its own (structure yes, doctrine no). (e) Predestination and election: left to other cards. RELATED IDS: card ids verified in ontology/entities/entities.jsonl (faith, grace, righteousness, justification, works, obedience, salvation). Theme ids are taken from ontology/themes/theme-hubs.json (deliverance, law_wisdom, judgment, mercy_restoration); the brief's example 'deliverance_salvation' does not exist in the repo files I could search, so please confirm which theme id the site actually uses before this is moved to ontology/questions/. UNRESOLVED: theme ids as above; the John 3:36 note relies on the site's own gloss of the Greek ('not obeying') and a reviewer should confirm it reads as a note and not as a verdict against the Berean.
